When you bake for your family, a small mistake is forgiven. When you bake for sale, every bun must look, taste and weigh the same as the last one, or customers stop coming back. The first habit of a production baker is simple: **weigh everything, store everything properly, and write it down.** This lesson shows you how.

Why weigh instead of using cups

A cup of flour can weigh very different amounts depending on whether you scoop it, spoon it in loosely or pack it down, and whether the flour has been sitting in a humid room. Two cups of flour from two different people can differ by a large amount. A **digital kitchen scale** that reads in 1 g steps removes that problem. Every recipe in this course is written in grams and millilitres for this reason.

Raising agents lose strength with age, heat and damp. A flat batch of buns or doughnuts wastes flour, oil and gas, so test them the evening before a big production day.

**Baking powder:** stir half a teaspoon into a few spoons of hot water. It should fizz strongly at once. Weak or no bubbles means replace it.

**Instant or active dry yeast:** stir 1 teaspoon of yeast and 1 teaspoon of sugar into about 60 ml of lukewarm water (warm to the touch, not hot). After about 10 minutes there should be a clear layer of foam. No foam means the yeast is dead.
Ingredient roles you will meet in this course

You do not need deep science to start, but knowing the job of each ingredient helps you fix problems. **Flour** gives structure. **Sugar** sweetens, browns the outside and keeps products soft. **Fat** (margarine or butter) makes products tender and helps them keep. **Eggs** bind, add richness and help set the structure. **Baking powder and baking soda** make gas quickly in the heat for buns, rock buns and banana bread. **Yeast** makes gas slowly at room temperature for doughnuts and bread. **Salt** gives flavour and controls yeast.

The method matters as much as the recipe. Over-mixing a muffin-method batter makes banana bread tough and full of tunnels. Under-kneading a yeast dough gives doughnuts that do not rise well. Warm, soft margarine in a rubbing-in recipe makes rock buns spread flat. Each recipe lesson will remind you of the right method.
Ovens: gas, electric and the pot oven

Most home gas and electric ovens are not accurate. The number on the dial is a guide, not a promise. An **oven thermometer** tells you the real temperature where your tray sits. Always **preheat** the oven, usually for 15 to 20 minutes, and check the thermometer before the tray goes in. If you do not have an oven, a **pot oven** works for small batches: a heavy pot with a lid, a layer of clean sand or a metal rack at the bottom so the tin does not touch the base, preheated on low to medium heat. It bakes more slowly and unevenly, so turn the tin during baking.
Worked example: checking an oven before a production day
For example, Ngozi in Enugu bought a second-hand gas cooker with an oven and wants to bake rock buns at 200 degrees Celsius.
She places an oven thermometer in the middle of the middle shelf, sets the dial to 180 and waits 20 minutes.
The thermometer reads 160 degrees Celsius, so her oven runs about 20 degrees low at that setting.
For rock buns at 200 degrees, she sets the dial higher, waits 20 minutes, and checks until the thermometer reads close to 200.
To find hot spots, she spreads 6 slices of white bread across one tray and bakes them for about 5 minutes at 180 degrees on the thermometer.
The slices at the back left are dark brown while the front slices are pale. She writes on an oven card: back left is hottest, turn trays halfway through.
Ngozi now knows her real dial setting and her oven's hot corner, so her first sale batch bakes evenly instead of half-burnt and half-pale.
Gas cylinder and cooker safety
Keep the gas cylinder upright, in a well-ventilated place, away from the heat of the burners and out of reach of children.
Check the hose and regulator regularly. Replace a hose that is cracked, hard or loose.
To check for a leak, brush soapy water on the joints with the cylinder valve open. Bubbles that grow mean gas is escaping. Never test with a flame.
When lighting a cooker or oven without automatic ignition, have the lit match or lighter ready at the burner before you turn the knob.
Turn the cylinder valve off at the end of every production day.
If you smell gas

Do not light anything and do not switch electrical items or lights on or off, because a spark can ignite gas. Turn off the cylinder valve if you can reach it safely, open doors and windows, get everyone out, and call a qualified gas technician or the fire service. Do not return until the smell is gone and the leak has been fixed.

With electric ovens and mixers, plug into a wall socket in good condition, do not overload extension boards, keep cables away from water and hot surfaces, and dry your hands before touching switches. If power from a generator or the grid changes suddenly, switch off and unplug appliances until it is stable.

Personal hygiene before you touch food

Wash hands with soap and clean running water, rubbing all surfaces including between fingers, thumbs and under nails, then rinse and dry on a clean towel or paper. WHO's handwashing guide takes about 40 to 60 seconds.
Wash again after using the toilet, touching raw egg or fish, handling money, using your phone, touching your hair or face, emptying the bin or changing a baby.
Tie back and cover your hair with a cap or scarf. Wear a clean apron used only for production.
Remove rings, bracelets and watches. Keep nails short and free of nail polish or false nails, which can chip into food.
Cover cuts and sores with a waterproof plaster, ideally a brightly coloured one so it is easy to spot if it falls off.
Do not produce food for sale if you have diarrhoea or vomiting. Many food businesses use the rule of staying away until at least 48 hours after symptoms stop.
Clean first, then sanitise

**Cleaning** removes visible dirt, flour paste and grease with hot soapy water. **Sanitising** kills most remaining germs, using very hot water or a food-safe sanitiser or diluted household bleach made up exactly as the label says for food-contact surfaces, then rinsed if the label says so. Sanitiser does not work on a dirty surface, so always clean first.
Worked example: a cleaning schedule for a shared kitchen
For example, Blessing in Port Harcourt bakes on Fridays and Saturdays in the kitchen her family uses every day.
Night before production: she clears the counter of family items, cleans and sanitises the worktop, checks that no food was left out overnight, and takes out the bin.
Start of production: hands washed, hair covered, apron on. She wipes the worktop again and washes bowls, scale bowl and trays in hot soapy water.
Between tasks: after making fish filling, she washes the chopping board, knife and her hands before touching pastry dough.
End of production: she lets frying oil cool, then washes all tools, cleans the cooker top, sweeps and mops, and empties the bin into a covered outside bin.
Weekly: she empties and wipes her ingredient containers, checks behind the cooker and under the sink for droppings or cockroaches, and washes aprons and towels.
Blessing's family can use the kitchen normally during the week, but production days start and end in a clean, checked space, and she ticks each line on a printed sheet taped inside a cupboard door.
Keeping pests out

Rats, mice, cockroaches, ants and flies spread germs and can ruin a whole sack of flour. Prevention is better than poison. Store all ingredients in sealed containers, wipe up flour and sugar spills straight away, keep a tight lid on the bin, and do not leave finished snacks uncovered. Seal holes around pipes and under doors where you can. If you must use insecticide or rat poison, never use it near food, utensils or ingredients, follow the label exactly, and keep it away from children.
Separate business and household risks

Keep children and pets out of the kitchen while you produce, both for hygiene and because hot oil and ovens are dangerous. Keep cleaning chemicals in their original labelled containers, stored below and away from food. Never put chemicals in old drink bottles.

Finally, think about water. If your water comes from a borehole, well or tanker and you are not sure of its quality, boil the water you use for dough and for rinsing tools that touch finished food, or use treated sachet or bottled water from a registered supplier.

Setting up the frying station
Use a deep, heavy-based pot on a stable burner, with the handle turned inwards so nobody knocks it.
Fill the pot no more than about one third to half full of oil. Food added to a full pot makes the oil rise and can overflow onto the flame.
Keep a lid that fits the pot, or a fire blanket, within arm's reach. Keep water, wet cloths and children away from the pot.
Put a draining tray lined with clean paper or a wire rack next to the pot, and a slotted spoon ready.
Heat the oil gradually on medium heat and check it with a frying thermometer. Never leave heating oil unattended, not even to answer the door.
Controlling oil temperature

Most fried snacks cook well with the oil somewhere between about **160 and 180 degrees Celsius**. Too cool, and the snack soaks up oil and becomes greasy. Too hot, and the outside browns or burns before the inside cooks. Each recipe gives a target. Adding a load of cold dough drops the temperature, so fry a few pieces at a time and let the oil recover before the next load. If oil starts to smoke, it is too hot: turn the heat down at once.

Without a thermometer, drop a small piece of dough into the oil. If it sinks and stays down, the oil is too cool. If it rises steadily with lively bubbles within a few seconds, the oil is about right for most snacks. If it browns almost instantly, it is too hot. A thermometer is still the better choice for consistent sale batches.
If the oil catches fire

Never throw water on burning oil: it turns to steam instantly and throws burning oil out of the pot. Turn off the heat if you can do it safely. Slide a fitting lid or a fire blanket over the pot to cut off the air, and leave it covered until the oil has cooled completely. Do not carry the pot outside. If the fire spreads, get everyone out, close the door and call the fire service. For any burn, cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes and seek medical help for anything larger than a small coin or on the face, hands or joints.
Looking after your oil

Oil can be reused a few times for the same kind of product if you look after it. After frying, let it cool completely, strain it through a fine sieve or clean cloth to remove crumbs, and store it covered in a cool dark place. Crumbs left in the oil burn next time and spoil both the oil and the flavour. Throw the oil away when it has become **dark and thick, smells sharp or stale, foams heavily, or starts smoking at its normal frying temperature**. Oil used for fish rolls will flavour buns and doughnuts, so keep separate oil for fish products.

Do not pour used oil down the sink or toilet: it sets and blocks drains. Pour cool oil into a container with a lid and put it in the general waste bin. The UK Food Standards Agency also advises aiming for a golden yellow colour or lighter when frying starchy foods, to reduce acrylamide, a substance that forms when these foods are browned too much. So avoid very dark, over-fried snacks.

Mix flour, sugar and yeast. Add salt on the other side of the bowl, then stir everything together.
Add the egg, margarine and most of the lukewarm milk. The milk should feel warm on your wrist, not hot, because very hot liquid kills yeast.

Judging proving by touch

Clocks help you plan, but dough tells you when it is ready. Press a floured finger gently into the dough about 1 cm deep. If the dent springs back quickly and completely, it needs more time. If it springs back slowly and leaves a small dent, it is ready. If it does not spring back at all, or the dough collapses, it is over-proved. Over-proved doughnuts absorb oil, taste yeasty and may sink. On a hot day, dough proves faster; on a cool, rainy morning, slower. Use cool water or milk on very hot days to slow it down.

Fish rolls are a favourite small chop: a crisp pastry rolled around seasoned fish. They are also a **higher-risk product**, because the fish filling is moist, protein-rich food that bacteria grow in quickly. A careless fish roll can make a customer sick. Done properly, fish rolls are safe, popular and sell at a higher price than plain snacks.

A fish
Fish fillings must be cooked through, carefully deboned and cooled quickly before they meet the pastry.
Step 1: the fish filling
Buy fresh fish such as mackerel (often called titus) from a clean seller. It should smell fresh, with firm flesh and bright eyes. Keep it cool and use it the same day.
Wash, then boil the fish with salt, onion and seasoning until fully cooked: the flesh flakes easily and is opaque all the way to the bone.
Let it cool just enough to handle, then remove skin and **every bone**. Run your fingers through the flaked fish twice. A bone in a snack is a choking hazard.
Fry chopped onion and blended pepper in a little oil, add the flaked fish and seasoning, and cook until hot all through and fairly dry. A wet filling makes soggy pastry and makes rolls burst.
Spread the filling thinly on a clean tray so it cools fast, cover it, and refrigerate once it stops steaming. Do not leave it at room temperature for more than 2 hours in total.
Never wrap warm filling

Warm filling softens the fat in the pastry and creates steam that bursts the roll. More importantly, a warm, covered, moist filling sitting in a hot kitchen is ideal for bacteria. Cool it quickly, keep it cold, and only take out as much as you will wrap in the next half hour. Keep raw fish, its knife and its board away from the pastry station.

Brush the far edge with water or beaten egg, roll up firmly and press the seam and the ends closed with a fork. Any gap lets oil in and filling out.
Fry at about 165 to 175 degrees Celsius for about 5 to 7 minutes, turning, until evenly golden. Fry a few at a time.
Drain and cool on a rack. Cut one open to check the pastry is cooked through and the filling is hot.

Coconut bread is soft, lightly sweet and smells wonderful, and it uses coconut that is cheap in many coastal and southern markets. Made as small rolls of equal weight, it is easy to price per piece and sells well to schools, offices and small shops. The method also teaches the yeast skills you will use for any soft bread.

Fresh coconut gives both the milk for the dough and the grated flesh for flavour.
Making fresh coconut milk
Crack a mature coconut, drain the water, and prise out the white flesh. Wash it and grate or chop it.
Set aside about 80 g of grated coconut for the dough.
Blend the rest with about 400 ml of warm (not boiling) safe water, then squeeze it through a clean cloth or fine sieve. You need about 300 ml of milk for one batch.

Fresh coconut milk spoils quickly. Use it within a few hours, keep it cool and covered, and throw it away if it smells sour. Canned or powdered coconut milk, made up as the pack says, is a reliable alternative.

Grated coconut
Coconut milk, lukewarm
about 300 ml
Mix flour, yeast and sugar, then add salt. Stir in the grated coconut.
Add margarine and most of the lukewarm coconut milk. Mix to a soft dough, adding the rest only if needed.
Knead for 10 to 12 minutes. Do the **windowpane test**: stretch a small piece between your fingers. If it stretches thin enough to let light through without tearing, the gluten is developed.
Cover and prove in a warm place until doubled, usually about 1 hour.
Press out the air, weigh the whole dough and divide into 12 equal pieces of about 80 g on the scale. Shape each into a tight ball by tucking the edges underneath.
Place on a greased tray about 2 cm apart, cover and prove 40 to 60 minutes until puffy and the finger test leaves a slow dent.
Brush with milk or beaten egg and bake at about 180 to 190 degrees Celsius (measured with your oven thermometer) for 15 to 20 minutes until golden.
Is it baked?

A fully baked roll is golden brown on top and underneath, and the base sounds hollow when you tap it. Squeeze gently at the side where rolls touched: it should spring back, not stay dented and damp. If you have a probe thermometer, the centre should read about 90 degrees Celsius or more. Under-baked bread is gummy inside and goes mouldy faster. Cool rolls on a rack, uncovered, for at least an hour before bagging. Bagging warm bread traps steam, which makes the crust wet and invites mould. Because this dough contains fresh coconut and coconut milk, it will not keep as long as plain bread. Run your own keeping test (Module 4) and plan to sell within a short window.
Scaling a recipe with a scaling factor

To make more, do not guess. Work out the **total dough weight** you need, divide by the total weight the recipe makes, and multiply every ingredient by that number. Our recipe makes 500 + 7 + 60 + 8 + 40 + 80 + 300 = 995 g of dough. Round the factor up slightly to cover dough that sticks to the bowl and table.

For example, Efe in Warri has an order for 30 coconut rolls of 80 g each.
Dough needed: 30 x 80 g = 2,400 g.
Scaling factor: 2,400 / 995 = 2.41. She rounds up to 2.5.
New amounts: flour 500 x 2.5 = 1,250 g; yeast 7 x 2.5 = 17.5 g; sugar 150 g; salt 20 g; margarine 100 g; grated coconut 200 g; coconut milk 750 ml.
New total: 2,487.5 g of dough, which gives 2,487.5 / 80 = 31 rolls, one spare to cut and check for doneness.
Her bowl is too small for 2.5 kg of dough, so she mixes it as two smaller doughs and bakes them in two rounds, 20 minutes apart.
Efe has exact quantities for her shopping list, 31 equal rolls, and a plan that fits her bowl and oven.

Small ingredients cause the biggest problems when scaled by eye. Weigh scaled yeast and salt on the scale, or count sachets (17.5 g is two and a half 7 g sachets). Too much salt slows the yeast; too much yeast makes bread rise fast and taste sour or yeasty.

Very ripe bananas with black-speckled skins are often sold cheaply because they will not last. For a baker, they are perfect: the riper the banana, the sweeter and more fragrant the bread. Banana bread needs no yeast and no kneading, keeps moist for a few days, and can be sold whole or by the slice.

A banana
Bananas with heavily speckled skins and soft flesh give the best flavour.
Choosing bananas
**Use:** bananas with yellow skins covered in brown or black spots, or fully dark skins, where the flesh inside is soft, sweet and creamy.
**Reject:** bananas with mould, a fermented or alcoholic smell, liquid leaking from the skin, or flesh that is grey and slimy.
Always weigh the peeled banana. Bananas vary greatly in size, so counting them gives inconsistent loaves.

Bicarbonate of soda (baking soda)
Margarine, melted and cooled
2 (about 100 g)
Ripe banana, peeled and mashed
Preheat the oven to about 175 degrees Celsius (check with your oven thermometer). Grease a large loaf tin (about 23 by 13 cm) and line the base with baking paper.
**Bowl 1 (dry):** whisk flour, bicarbonate of soda and salt together so the soda is spread evenly.
**Bowl 2 (wet):** mash the bananas, then mix in the melted margarine, sugar and beaten eggs.
Pour the wet mix into the dry and fold with a spatula **only until no dry flour shows**. A few small lumps are fine. Over-mixing develops gluten and makes a tough loaf with tunnels.
Pour into the tin, level the top and bake for about 50 to 60 minutes.

Test with a clean skewer or thin knife in the centre. It is done when it comes out clean or with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter. If the top browns too fast before the centre is done, cover it loosely with foil.
Cool 10 minutes in the tin, then turn out onto a rack and cool completely before slicing.
Why baking soda, not baking powder

Bicarbonate of soda needs an acid to make gas. Ripe banana supplies some acid, and soda also helps the loaf brown. Too much soda gives a soapy or metallic taste and a very dark crumb, so weigh it carefully rather than adding an extra pinch.
Turning loaves into slices for sale

Selling by the slice often earns more per loaf than selling whole, and customers can buy a small treat with their tea. Cool the loaf completely (warm loaves crumble and sweat in their wrapping), trim the two thin end pieces for tasting samples, then cut about 10 even slices with a long serrated knife. Wrap each slice in food-grade film or put it in a small clear bag and seal it. Banana bread is moist, so in humid weather it can go mouldy within a few days. Run your own keeping test before you decide on a sell-by date.

She buys 12 overripe bananas, peels and weighs them: 960 g of flesh. She uses 900 g and eats the rest.
She mixes the batter as three separate bowls of one loaf each, so every loaf gets the same gentle folding, and bakes all three tins together, checking they do not touch each other or the oven walls.
Her oven's back left corner is hottest (from her oven card), so she swaps the tins around after 30 minutes.
After cooling, she cuts each loaf into 10 slices: 3 x 10 = 30 slices, and keeps the trimmed ends as tasting samples.
Yetunde delivers 30 even, individually wrapped slices every Friday and knows exactly how many bananas to buy.

10 g (2 level teaspoons)
Raisins or grated coconut
a pinch to half a teaspoon

about 1 to 2 tablespoons (15 to 30 ml)

Mix flour and baking powder. Rub in the **cold** margarine with your fingertips until the mixture looks like fine breadcrumbs. Lift and let it fall to keep it cool and airy.
Stir in sugar, nutmeg and raisins or coconut.
Add the beaten egg and just enough milk to make a **stiff** dough. If it is soft and sticky, the buns will spread and lose their rocky shape.
Using two forks, place 12 rough heaps of about 45 to 50 g on the tray, 3 cm apart. Do not smooth them: the rough surface gives the crunchy peaks.

Freshly grated coconut
Water
about 60 ml
Grease a tray or a clean banana leaf and two metal spoons. Put a bowl of cold water nearby for testing, and keep children out of the kitchen.
Heat sugar and water in a heavy pot over medium heat, stirring only until the sugar dissolves. Then stop stirring and let it boil.
Watch closely. When the syrup turns a light amber or golden colour, lower the heat and add the coconut.

Hot sugar burns badly

Cooking sugar becomes far hotter than boiling water, and it sticks to skin. Wear long sleeves, use a long-handled spoon, never taste from the pot and never touch the mixture until it has cooled. If hot sugar touches skin, cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes. Do not try to peel off stuck sugar, and do not put butter, oil, toothpaste or raw egg on a burn. Get medical help for large burns or burns on the face, hands or joints.

A good product only becomes income when it reaches the customer fresh, honestly labelled and at a price that covers every cost. Packaging has three jobs: keep the product clean and safe, keep it in good condition until it is eaten, and tell the customer what it is and who made it. The right pack depends on the product. Doughnuts, fish rolls, bread and coconut candy each fail in a different way if packed wrongly.

Use only food-grade packaging

Use bags, boxes and film sold for food. Do not use printed newspaper, cement or chemical sacks, or bags that held detergent or other non-food items, because ink and residues can transfer to food. Store clean packaging covered, away from dust, pests and chemicals.
Cool first, then pack

The most common packaging mistake is packing too soon. Warm snacks release steam. In a closed bag, that steam condenses into water droplets, the crust goes soft and mould grows faster. Cool products on a rack, uncovered or loosely covered with a clean cloth against flies, until they feel cool to the touch all the way through. Fried snacks usually need about 30 minutes; loaves need an hour or more. Fish rolls are the exception to slow cooling: their filling is perishable, so cool them just enough to pack, keep them covered and get them to the customer quickly.
What an honest label says
**Product name**, for example "Coconut Bread Rolls".
**Ingredients**, listed from the largest amount to the smallest by weight.
**Allergens** clearly highlighted, for example in bold: wheat (gluten), egg, milk, fish, groundnuts or other nuts.
**Quantity**: number of pieces or net weight.
**Date made and best before date**, set from your own keeping test.
**Your business name and phone number**, so a customer can reach you.

If you plan to supply supermarkets or sell pre-packaged products through shops, NAFDAC registration is usually required for pre-packaged food in Nigeria, and NAFDAC has an MSME route for small producers. Check the current requirements on the NAFDAC website. Never print a NAFDAC number you have not been issued.
Setting your own sell-by date

Keeping time depends on your recipe, your kitchen and the weather, so run a simple **keeping test** rather than copying someone else's date. Pack a few pieces exactly as you would for sale, store them as a customer would, and check them every day for smell, texture, taste and any sign of mould. Your best before date should be shorter than the day the product first went off, to give a safety margin. Repeat the test in the rainy season, when humidity speeds up mould. Store packed products in a cool, clean, covered place, away from direct sun, the cooker and the floor, until they leave your kitchen. A plastic crate with a lid kept on a table works well for small batches.

Coconut candy made the day before, cooled, wrapped in twists and kept in an airtight tub.

Delivery leaves at 3:15 pm. She tells the host to serve the fish rolls during the party and not keep leftovers in the warm hall overnight.
Everything arrives fresh: candy crisp, buns cool and firm, fish rolls made last and delivered within about 2 hours of frying.

The fix is to cost the **whole production day**, not only the flour and sugar. Gas, frying oil, packaging, transport, pieces you cannot sell and your own hours are all real costs.

All naira figures here are example prices chosen to make the arithmetic clear. Prices change often and differ between cities and markets. Always replace them with what you actually paid, from your own receipts.
The six cost groups
**Ingredients** for each batch, from your recipe weights and the price per kg you paid.
**Frying oil** used up: oil absorbed by the snacks and oil you top up or throw away.
**Fuel**: gas or electricity. To estimate gas, note how many hours of burner use one cylinder refill gives you, then divide the refill price by those hours.
**Packaging and labels**, counted per piece.
**Transport and delivery**, including your own trips to buy ingredients if they are only for this production.
**Labour**: your hours and any helper's. If you do not pay yourself, your business is not really making money; it is using your free time.
Then allow for **wastage**: pieces you cut open to test, broken or misshapen pieces, and tasting samples. Divide costs by the number of pieces you can actually sell, not the number you made.

Worked example: costing a production day

For example, Bisi in Ilorin makes 2 batches of buns (48 pieces) and 2 batches of doughnuts (30 pieces) on a Tuesday. She keeps 2 of each for testing and samples, so she can sell 46 buns and 28 doughnuts.
Ingredients: buns 2 x N2,121.50 = N4,243; doughnuts 2 x N1,942.50 = N3,885. Total N8,128.
Oil used: 1.5 litres x N2,500 = N3,750. Gas: her refill lasts about 30 burner hours and costs N15,000, so N500 per hour; 4 hours = N2,000.
Packaging: 78 bags x N20 = N1,560; labels 78 x N10 = N780. Delivery: N1,000. Her labour: 6 hours x N700 = N4,200.

Shared cost per sellable piece: 13,290 / 74 = about N180. Bun ingredients per piece: 4,243 / 46 = about N92, so a bun costs about N272. Doughnut ingredients per piece: 3,885 / 28 = about N139, so a doughnut costs about N318.
She prices buns at N350 and doughnuts at N400. If all sell: 46 x 350 + 28 x 400 = N27,300. Profit after paying herself: 27,300 - 21,418 = N5,882.
Bisi now knows that copying a neighbour's price of N200 per bun would have lost money, and that her prices of N350 and N400 cover every cost and pay her wage.
Why bigger production days cost less per piece

Some costs grow with every piece (ingredients, bags, labels). Others grow much more slowly (heating the oil, delivery trips, setting up and cleaning). If Bisi doubles to 4 batches of each, with 2.5 litres of oil, 6 hours of gas, 156 bags and labels, one delivery trip and 9 hours of labour, her day costs N37,486 for 148 sellable pieces: about N253 per piece on average instead of about N289. At the same prices, her profit rises to N17,114, but only if she has orders for all of them. Never bake more just to lower the cost per piece if the extra pieces will not sell.
Re-cost every time prices move

When flour, sugar, oil or gas prices change, update your costing sheet the same week. A price that was profitable last month can quietly become a loss. Tell regular customers early and politely when you must raise prices.

Selling is where many good bakers lose money: baking too much on a quiet day, too little on a busy one, giving credit that is never paid, or being tricked by a fake payment alert. A simple system of pre-orders, records and clear rules for unsold stock protects your profit and your reputation.

A simple pre-order system
Set up **WhatsApp Business** with your business name, phone number, location and opening hours. Add each product to the **catalogue** with a clear photo, price, piece count and allergen note.
Choose a **cut-off time** for orders, for example 6:00 pm the evening before production. Post it on your status and repeat it in every order reply.
Write every order in one place: customer name, products and quantities, delivery or pickup time, address, amount and payment status.
For large or special orders, ask for part payment before you buy ingredients, for example half. Explain your policy clearly before the customer commits.
The evening before production, add up all orders to set your batch numbers, then add a small number of extra pieces for walk-in buyers based on your sales record.
Confirm payment in your own bank app

Fake transfer screenshots and fake SMS alerts are common scams. Before you hand over goods paid by transfer, open your own bank, Opay, Moniepoint or other account app and confirm that the money has actually arrived. Do not rely on a screenshot or a text message, however urgent the customer seems.
Selling hygienically at a stall or on delivery
Display snacks in a covered, clean container or glass display box, never open to dust and flies.
Serve with tongs or a clean paper sheet, not bare hands, especially after touching money.
If you can, let a helper handle cash while you handle food; if alone, use tongs and keep hand sanitiser at the stall.
Carry deliveries in a clean, closed carrier, kept out of direct sun and away from fuel or chemicals in the vehicle.
When supplying a shop or school tuck shop, agree in writing on price per piece, delivery days, payment terms and what happens to unsold perishable items.
Keep a daily sales record

A notebook page or simple spreadsheet per day is enough. Record, for each product: pieces made, pieces sold, pieces given as samples, pieces left over and what happened to them, plus money received and how (cash or transfer). From this record you can calculate **sell-through**: pieces sold divided by pieces made, as a percentage. Sell-through close to 100% early in the day may mean you could make more; low sell-through means you are making too many or selling in the wrong place.
Worked example: using sell-through to adjust production
For example, Zainab in Abuja sells doughnuts at a bus stop near offices on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. She makes 60 each day and records her sales for a week.
Monday: made 60, sold 48. Sell-through 48 / 60 = 80%. Twelve left over.
Wednesday: made 60, sold 57. Sell-through 57 / 60 = 95%.
Friday: made 60, sold all 60 by 11:00 am. Sell-through 100%, and customers were turned away.
She checks the same pattern for three more weeks before changing anything.
When it repeats, she makes 3 full batches plus a half batch on Mondays (45 + 7 = 52 doughnuts, close to the 48 she sells) and adds one batch on Fridays, making 60 + 15 = 75.
Zainab cuts Monday waste, sells more on Fridays, and bases each change on four weeks of written records instead of a guess.
Rules for unsold stock
**Fish rolls and anything with a perishable filling:** do not hold over to sell the next day unless they were chilled promptly and you are sure they are safe; when in doubt, throw them away.
**Breads, buns and cakes:** if still within your tested best before date and in good condition, sell them as clearly labelled "yesterday's bake" at a discount, never mixed in with fresh stock.
**Never** sell anything with mould, a sour or stale smell, or a damaged pack, and never re-label old stock with a new date.
Record every leftover and what you did with it. Leftovers are information: they tell you how to plan the next day.

Finally, look after regular customers. Answer messages politely and quickly, keep promises on delivery times, and handle complaints by listening, apologising, replacing or refunding where you were at fault, and writing down what you will change. A customer who complains is giving you a chance to keep her.
